ModelCharacter: The original and most traditional Albin 28 TE layout: a rugged Downeast-style diesel cruiser/fisherman with its single engine beneath a cushioned cockpit box, leaving the machinery close to the hull's intended balance point and preserving a larger quarter berth below.
DesignLineage: The Albin 28 Tournament Express ran from 1993–2007 and became one of the company's best-known U.S.-built powerboats.
The Engine Box arrangement was the original configuration and dominated production before the Flush Deck option appeared in 2003.
Both Engine Box and Flush Deck versions use the same 28 TE modified-V hull, 10-foot beam and Downeast fishing/cruising mission.
The later Newport Edition was a seating/finish evolution of the 28 TE rather than a separate hull.
OwnershipCharacter: A strong single-diesel cruiser with good parts knowledge and owner support. The engine box takes cockpit floor area but generally provides straightforward machinery access; engine installation, fuel tanks, core condition and decades of upgrades remain the main survey variables.

ModelCharacter: A highly regarded Spencer Lincoln-designed Maine lobsterboat hull that became a favorite foundation for custom Downeast cruisers. The BHM 32 combines a deep forefoot, built-down hull, single inboard diesel and full keel with enough beam and displacement for serious coastal cruising or commercial work.
DesignLineage: The BHM 32 is a Spencer Lincoln Downeast design built in Maine and commonly finished by multiple yards.
Surviving boats are marketed both simply as BHM 32 and as Flye Point 32 cruisers depending on builder/finisher.
Modern brokerage references also connect the design to the Seaworthy/BHM line, reflecting continued use of the underlying hull concept.
Because finishing yard, propulsion and accommodations vary substantially, B-Atlas treats BHM 32 as the hull/model family and preserves Flye Point 32 as an alias/configuration.
OwnershipCharacter: A very strong owner-operated platform when finished well: single diesel, protected running gear and commercial-grade hull form. The challenge is non-standardization—survey quality of the finish yard's deckhouse, wiring, tanks, insulation and systems matters as much as the hull itself.

ModelCharacter: A broad-beam trunk-cabin Island Gypsy designed as a deliberate return to traditional trawler styling, but with enough power and hard aft chines for moderate semi-displacement speeds. It combines two- or three-stateroom accommodation with wide walkaround decks and a full teak interior.
DesignLineage: Powerboat Guide documents the 40 Classic as a distinct model, with a significant exterior redesign in 1995.
The redesigned generation replaced the earlier stepped sheer with a straighter, more contemporary sheer and revised flybridge.
The original three-stateroom arrangement was later replaced by a roomier two-stateroom layout.
The 40 Classic shares hull dimensions with other Island Gypsy 40 variants but is distinct from the 40 Sedan, Europa and Flush Aft Deck layouts.

ModelVariations.Description: Kadey-Krogen models evolved through multiple layouts and equipment packages; the 38 Cutter is a distinct sailing/motorsailing design rather than a conventional Krogen trawler.

ModelCharacter: A large raised-pilothouse ocean trawler with deep forefoot, ballasted full-displacement hull and genuine two- or three-stateroom liveaboard capability. The North Sea emphasizes traditional offshore security and volume rather than the more contemporary refinements of the later 48 AE.
DesignLineage: The Krogen 48 North Sea was produced from the mid-1990s through 2010 as a semi-custom long-range passagemaker.
Standard walkaround and Widebody arrangements were available, with the Widebody sacrificing the port side deck for greater salon volume.
The North Sea shares Krogen's full-displacement design philosophy but is a distinct older model from the later Krogen 48 AE.
More than 50 North Sea examples were built, establishing it as one of Krogen's significant large-model families.
OwnershipCharacter: A true long-range liveaboard yacht with major tankage, stabilizers and large-system maintenance requirements. Single-engine propulsion remains efficient and straightforward, but haul-out, dockage, coatings, hydraulics and hotel systems are firmly yacht-scale.

ModelVariations.Name: Vega configuration families
ModelVariations.Description: Willard used the same hull families for distinct Nomad, Voyager, Horizon, Searcher and other configurations. “Vega” identifies a hull family rather than one universal layout.

ModelCharacter: The original production-fiberglass Willard trawler: a Bill Garden-designed double-ended full-displacement cruiser with a ballasted keel, single diesel, flybridge sedan layout and unusually serious offshore proportions for a 36-footer.
DesignLineage: Bill Garden designed the Vega 36 in 1961 for Vega Marine, with construction subcontracted to Willard Boat Works.
Hulls 1–25 were marketed as Vega 36s; after Willard acquired the mold, later hulls were marketed as Willard Vega 36s.
Thirty-nine hulls were produced through 1970: 28 Standard Cruisers, 6 Aft Pilothouse boats, 5 motorsailers and one full sailing version according to the owner archive.
B-Atlas now uses the Standard Cruiser as the canonical powerboat identity because the prior generic 'Vega 36 family' record mixed materially different power and sail configurations.
OwnershipCharacter: A remarkably substantial old fiberglass cruiser with simple single-diesel machinery and excellent displacement efficiency. Its age is the central issue: tankage, original electrical systems, windows, deck hardware and more than sixty years of repairs or modifications require careful hull-specific inspection.
